Agreed. Even as a Chinese I understand why NEP was necessary back then, a minority race holding that much wealth is a country ready to explode from racial infighting. But nowadays it’s different, Chinese salaries are the only race that’s decreasing year on year, and the cause is brain drain, so many educated people rather leave overseas even though their heart stays in Malaysia, but economically it makes no sense for them to stay and it’s sad. 

Not to mention nowadays most Malays especially in urban areas are a healthy middle class and many run businesses in the upper class. More and more NEP policies only drives productivity down, because many know they can Rempit non stop then go to work without doing work and still live a healthy life, this staggers the economy and people often talk about the rising debt, well to pay for subsidies with money you don’t have you have to borrow more and more money.. this also creates the melayu malas stereotype, no single race in the world is inherently better than others, and melayu didn’t get that stereotype because they were born like that but rather they can live like that without repercussions.. 

the same issue is happening in western countries. High unemployment benefits so all the drug addicts and homeless people are actually more comfortable and making more money being homeless and claiming benefit than finding a job at McDonald’s..

NEP should still exist but it shouldn’t fully target race anymore.. it should target income B40 household are still eligible, but it makes no sense that a Malay director making millions can still get high interest savings, discounted bumi houses etc..

replies.author: @firdausm3617
replies.text:
Indonesia has more oil reserves than Malaysia, yet its national oil company, PERTAMINA, has faced recurring financial losses, corruption scandals and mismanagement. On the other hand, Singapore has virtually no natural oil resources but has become one of the wealthiest countries in Southeast Asia.

So, having oil doesn't automatically make a country rich. What matters is how well the country's resources are managed, the quality of its institutions, and whether its leaders are transparent and accountable. Even if the Philippines has oil reserves, there's no guarantee it could develop Sabah's oil resources as effectively as Malaysia has developed its petroleum industry through PETRONAS.
